To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
increased phenotypic (i.e. developmental) plasticity to climate may have boosted the invasion success of polyploid Centauea stoebe.

(1) European tetraploidy is associated with increased levels of phenological and eco-physiological plasticity, (2) phenotypic plasticities are adaptive in response to climatic conditions, (3) invasive North American tetra-ploids show no increased plasticity as compared with native European tetraplo ids and (4) phenotypic differences between diploids and European tetraplo ids are not associated with differences in plasticity.

1) Polyploid plants may show increased phenotypic flexibility in response to environmental change, which could in part explain their increased invasiveness; 2) In particular traits associated with rapid plant growth and fast phenology may show increased plasticity in polyploid as compared to diploid plants; 3) The increased plasticity may be adaptive in the new environment, which suggests that it may have contributed to increased invasiveness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolutionary and ecological processes that are involved in the invasion success of C. stoebo.
the role of phenology in the invasion of alien species.
the role of phenotypes and their plasticity for plant invasions.

the increased plasticity of the tetraploid plants may have been an important factor in their success in the invaded range.
the increased phenotypic flexibility of polyploids may have boosted the success of the invasive tetraploidy in C. stoebes.
polyploids are not per se invasive, but that their phenotypic plastic response may be a key component of their invasive success.
